paras: The Pittsville church shooting was an attack in October 1888 in which a crowd of armed young white men rode up to a Black church at Pittsville, in Fort Bend County, Texas, called the congregation out and fired into it. Lamar Johnson was killed and Taylor Randon was wounded. The Galveston News called it a political assassination and blamed the Jay Bird Club, a new Democratic organization, while a leading Fort Bend Democrat denied that politics played any part.

Pittsville lay ten miles north of Richmond, the home of the Fort Bend County sheriff. According to the Galveston News, the shooting came amid a "bitter political feeling" in the county, and "unprovoked political assassinations" had become frequent in that section of the state. The same paper held "the Jay Bird Club, a new Democratic organization in Fort Bend County," directly responsible for the condition of affairs there.

On a Saturday night, most likely 13 October since a Texas news digest carried the story on 16 October, a party of armed men rode up to the church at Pittsville. In the Galveston News account, the men were "young white men of Pittsville" who called the people out of the church and fired into them. Lamar Johnson was killed, and Taylor Randon was wounded; the earlier digest said one was killed and "several others" were wounded, without naming anyone. The News described both named men as well known in the county and "good, law-abiding citizens," and no accusation against them is reported.

Randon fled the county for safety. The county sheriff, Jim Garvey of Richmond, was in Galveston the day before the News printed its account, but no arrest, inquest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and the attackers were not named.

The first report was a single line in a digest of Texas news in the San Antonio Daily Light, which called the event "a row" and gave no names or cause. The Galveston News treated it at length as a political crime, calling it one of those "unprovoked, cold-blooded murders" committed by men who could not appreciate the crime of murder "when the victim chances to be a negro." The News also observed that the killing accomplished nothing directly except "the killing of one more negro" and the intimidation it was meant to produce.

Northern papers took up the Galveston text in the days before the November election. The New-York Tribune reprinted it on 28 October under the headline "Keeping the South Solid by Murder," and the Cleveland Gazette ran the full text under the same headline on 3 November, on a page of news about colored Republican clubs preparing for the election. In Texas, the Houston Post answered with a Fort Bend view, reprinted by the Austin Weekly Statesman on 1 November.

The cause of the shooting was disputed. The Galveston News gave political feeling as "the only cause assigned" and blamed the Jay Bird Club. Capt. P. E. Pearson, a Fort Bend lawyer described as a leading Democrat of the county, told the Houston Post that the killing "was not the result of political feeling" and that a statement by "Randall Taylor," probably the wounded Randon, was believed correct as to the cause; that statement does not appear in the coverage.

bases: A band of armed white men rode up to a Black church, called the congregation out and fired into the crowd, killing one man and wounding one or several others (A1, A2).

A Texas news digest (A1) and the Galveston News account (A2, A3) independently report the shooting at a Pittsville church, and a Houston Post item (A4) confirms the killing of Lamar Johnson near Pittsville while disputing its cause.
